title: Pardons Dinesh D’Souza
description_medium: On May 31, 2018, President Donald Trump granted conservative commentator Dinesh D’Souza a full pardon. D’Souza had pleaded guilty to campaign-contribution fraud in a New York Senate race and received five years’ probation, eight months of community confinement, weekly community service and a $30,000 fine. The White House described him as a victim of selective prosecution, a characterization it attributed to Trump.
description_long: Trump granted Dinesh D’Souza a full pardon on May 31, 2018. The conservative author and filmmaker had pleaded guilty in 2014 to arranging illegal campaign contributions for Wendy Long, a Republican challenging New York Senator Kirsten Gillibrand. News accounts reported that D’Souza arranged for two associates to contribute $10,000 each, exceeding campaign-finance limits. The Justice Department’s record lists the offense as campaign contribution fraud and records five years of probation, including eight months of community confinement and one day of community service each week, plus a $30,000 fine. The White House’s announcement characterized D’Souza, in Trump’s view, as a victim of selective prosecution. It also said he accepted responsibility and completed community service teaching English to people seeking citizenship. Those points were the administration’s stated grounds; they do not change the underlying guilty plea or establish that the prosecution was politically motivated. The pardon was a complete executive clemency grant, distinct from the sentence he had received in federal court.

rationale: The Justice Department record establishes the pardon, offense and sentence. The White House stated Trump’s view that D’Souza faced selective prosecution and cited his acceptance of responsibility and community service.

title: Pardons Michael Milken
description_medium: President Donald Trump pardoned financier Michael Milken on February 18, 2020, one of seven full pardons announced that day. Milken had pleaded guilty in a federal securities-fraud case and served prison time; the Justice Department lists conspiracy, securities fraud, mail fraud, tax fraud and related offenses, as well as a $200 million fine and extensive community service. The White House cited his later philanthropic work.
description_long: On February 18, 2020, President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Michael Milken, the former Drexel Burnham Lambert financier associated with the 1980s junk-bond market. Milken’s federal case ended in a guilty plea to securities, mail and tax fraud, conspiracy, false SEC filings and related offenses. The Justice Department records an amended prison term of 24 months, three years of supervised release conditioned on 5,400 hours of community service, and a $200 million fine. Trump’s action was one of seven pardons announced that day, alongside four commutations. In its announcement, the White House praised Milken’s role in financing emerging businesses and pointed to his later medical-research, education and charitable work; it said post-conviction efforts to improve communities informed the clemency decision. The Los Angeles Times reported that numerous prominent business and political figures had supported a pardon, including Rudy Giuliani, who had led the federal investigation that resulted in Milken’s prosecution. The pardon did not erase the historical conviction. The case record, the administration’s account of Milken’s later philanthropy, and the supporters’ advocacy provide separate context for understanding the grant; the announcement itself did not adjudicate the underlying case anew.
source_access_notes: Read the Justice Department clemency record and archived White House or contemporaneous reporting for the event. For the McGahn episode, also read Mueller report Volume II.
rationale: The February 18 grant was a full pardon. DOJ supplies the offense and sentence history; the White House supplied a philanthropic rationale, while the Los Angeles Times documented prominent supporters including Milken’s former prosecutor Rudy Giuliani.

title: Pardons Rep. Duncan Hunter
description_medium: On December 22, 2020, Trump granted former Representative Duncan Hunter a full pardon, less than a month before Hunter was due to report to prison. Hunter had pleaded guilty in 2019 to one count of misusing campaign funds and was sentenced to 11 months for the federal offense. The White House said the pardon came at the request of members of Congress.
description_long: President Donald Trump granted former California Representative Duncan Hunter a full pardon on December 22, 2020. Hunter had pleaded guilty in 2019 to one count of misusing campaign funds after prosecutors accused him and his then-wife of using campaign money for personal expenses. In March 2020, a federal judge sentenced Hunter to 11 months in prison, scheduled to begin in January 2021; the pardon came before he started that term. The Justice Department lists the offense as conspiracy to commit offenses and records the 11-month sentence followed by three years of supervised release. The White House said the grant was requested by members of Congress and highlighted Hunter’s service as a Marine and his combat deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. The Los Angeles Times reported that Hunter had admitted using more than $150,000 in campaign donations for personal purchases, including video games, dog food, hotel rooms and travel for family pets. That account explains the conduct underlying the case; the White House’s stated rationale describes the administration’s explanation for clemency, not a judicial finding about the appropriateness of the pardon.
source_access_notes: Read the Justice Department clemency record and archived White House or contemporaneous reporting for the event. For the McGahn episode, also read Mueller report Volume II.
rationale: Public clemency records establish the pardon, conviction, sentence and impending prison start. The White House attributed the grant to congressional requests and Hunter’s military service; contemporaneous reporting details the admitted campaign-fund misuse.

title: Trump urges Russia to find Clinton’s missing emails
description_medium: At a July 27, 2016, press conference in Doral, Florida, then-candidate Donald Trump addressed Russia while discussing Hillary Clinton’s deleted emails and the recently disclosed Democratic National Committee hack. He said he hoped Russia could find the missing emails and suggested the press might reward it. Clinton’s campaign called the appeal an encouragement of espionage; Trump later said foreign countries should share any emails with the FBI.
description_long: During a press conference in Doral, Florida, on July 27, 2016, Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump publicly appealed to Russia to find emails Hillary Clinton had deleted from a private server. The remarks came days after the Democratic National Committee disclosed a hack of its files and while Trump and Clinton were campaigning for the presidency. Trump said, “Russia, if you’re listening,” then said he hoped Russia could find 30,000 missing emails and suggested the press would reward it. He also said Russia might already have them. Clinton’s campaign responded that he was encouraging a foreign power to conduct espionage against a political opponent and called the matter a national-security issue. Trump’s running mate, Mike Pence, later said that if Russia was interfering in the election, the United States would impose serious consequences. Trump subsequently tweeted that any country or person holding Clinton’s emails should share them with the FBI. The public statements are documented; they do not by themselves establish whether Russia acted because of the appeal or whether Trump coordinated privately with Russian officials.
source_access_notes: Read the Justice Department clemency record and archived White House or contemporaneous reporting for the event. For the McGahn episode, also read Mueller report Volume II.
rationale: The Doral transcript records Trump’s appeal and later statement about sending emails to the FBI. TIME reports the campaign response and Pence’s public warning; neither source establishes a private agreement or causation.

title: Report says Trump directed McGahn to seek Mueller’s removal
description_medium: On January 25, 2018, The New York Times reported that President Donald Trump had directed White House Counsel Don McGahn to tell the Justice Department to remove Special Counsel Robert Mueller in June 2017. McGahn did not relay the request and decided he would resign rather than carry it out. Trump disputed the reporting the next day. Mueller’s later report examined the episode in its obstruction inquiry.
description_long: The New York Times reported on January 25, 2018, that President Donald Trump had directed White House Counsel Don McGahn to have Special Counsel Robert Mueller removed the previous June. According to that account, Trump wanted McGahn to ask the Justice Department to dismiss Mueller; McGahn did not deliver the request and decided he would resign rather than take part. The report emerged while Mueller was investigating Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible obstruction of justice. Trump rejected the story as “fake news” the next day. The Justice Department’s 2019 Mueller report later confirmed that Trump called McGahn on June 17, 2017, and directed him to contact the acting attorney general, say Mueller had conflicts of interest, and secure Mueller’s removal. McGahn did not carry out the direction. The report said substantial evidence supported the conclusion that Trump had gone beyond asking officials to review alleged conflicts and sought Mueller’s removal. It also recorded that, after the January 2018 coverage, McGahn would not deny the accounts because he believed they were accurate. This entry records the public revelation and subsequent documentary corroboration, while keeping Trump’s denial and the special counsel’s analysis visible. Mueller’s report was an investigative account, not a court judgment on criminal liability.

title.corrected: Report says Trump directed McGahn to seek Mueller’s removal
title.reason: The entry date is the 2018 report; the described directive was alleged to have occurred in June 2017, and Trump disputed the report.

source_access_notes: Read the Justice Department clemency record and archived White House or contemporaneous reporting for the event. For the McGahn episode, also read Mueller report Volume II.
rationale: The January 25 report concerned an alleged June 2017 directive; Trump denied the account. The later Mueller report discussed McGahn’s recollection and the president’s effort to have him deny the reported direction.
